subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The Startup Graveyard
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Startup Graveyard usable.

hook.text: Dozens of self-driving startups raised billions of dollars promising full autonomy within five years.

buildup.text: Argo AI, backed by Ford and Volkswagen, had 2,000 employees and seemed destined to lead.

discovery.text: In 2022, both Ford and VW pulled funding and Argo shut down overnight, stunning the industry.

twist.text: They weren't alone—Aurora, Motional, and others burned through cash without reaching profitability.

climax.text: The self-driving gold rush left a trail of failed companies that underestimated the hardest problems.

punchline.text: Billions in funding couldn't buy the last mile of autonomy.

quiz.question: What happened to Argo AI, the Ford/VW-backed self-driving company?

details.summary: Dozens of autonomous vehicle startups have failed or been acquired at steep losses, including Argo AI, Drive.ai, and Zoox, revealing that self-driving technology is far more expensive and difficult than projected.
details.whyItMatters: The startup graveyard shows that autonomous driving cannot be solved with venture capital alone. The staggering costs and technical complexity have winnowed the field to a few well-funded survivors.
takeaways: Argo AI shut down despite billions from Ford and Volkswagen
Many AV startups underestimated the difficulty of edge cases
Surviving companies have pivoted to narrower use cases

faq.question: Why have so many autonomous vehicle startups failed?
faq.answer: Building self-driving technology requires billions in sustained investment with no near-term revenue. The technical complexity of achieving reliable autonomy was vastly underestimated, and investors lost patience as timelines slipped.

faq.question: Which autonomous vehicle companies have the best chance of surviving?
faq.answer: Waymo, backed by Alphabet's deep pockets, and companies with focused use cases like trucking or controlled environments are seen as most likely to survive. Companies needing external funding face the highest risk.
